colour and brittleness of the grass roots." Still, the
readers of worthy Sylvanus Urban were not quite
satisfied, and in the very next magazine appeared a
speculation of "C," on the likelihood of the fairy
circles being vestiges of trenches dug by the ancient
Britons, and "used either in celebrating some of their
sports, or in paying divine honours to some of their
imaginary deities. These trenches," he says, "gra-
dually filling up by the annual decay of vegetables,
and being necessarily lighter than the adjoining land,
and consequently more retentive of water, and less
capable of enjoying the solar influence till later in the
year, will not only be rendered more fertile, but the
grass growing upon them more perceptible than the
neighbouring parts of the field, especially in the
autumnal quarter."
Mr Eeles's explanation was now combated by "M.
C.," of Cornwall, who had fairy rings in a bowling-
green, where cattle, of course, never were, much less
stakes for the allayment of prurience in the neck;
also by "B. L. A.," who never had seen a fairy ring
with a scrubbing post in the centre; and, thirdly, by
no less a person than Sir David Dalrymple, author
of the Annals of Scotland, who says, that, in his
garden at New Hailes, near Edinburgh, he has had
fairy circles of twenty years' endurance, where there
had never been either posts or cattle in the memory
of man.
At this crisis of the argument, there appeared in
the Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh
a paper by the celebrated Dr Hutton, describing some
appearances of the character of fairy circles, which
he had observed in the year 1776 on the hill called
Arthur's Seat, near Edinburgh. In various parts of
that mountain, there were tracts of withered herbage,
of about ten inches broad, defined generally by borders
of bright green grass, and in some places broken by
patches of the same from one to two hundred yards
long, and generally affecting a circular figure, or being
segments of circles. These appearances, though recent,
or of that year's production, had certainly been pre-
ceded by others of the same kind; for, parallel to each
tract of withered grass, there was another perfectly
similar, on the side towards the centre of the circle,
separated by a narrow stripe of green herbage, and
presenting a black appearance, as if the grass which
it originally bore were completely decayed. Still
further inward, was a belt of luxuriantly green grass,
which Dr Hutton supposed to be the newly-acquired
cover of what had last year been a decayed tract, be-
cause plants of the same colour were beginning to
make their appearance here and there on the back
ground of the decayed tract of the present year. 
Thus
it was evident, he thought, that those stripes were
successively formed; and, indeed, he could in some
places distin distinguish traces of five or six, by the grada-
tion of colour observable in the grass growing on them,
between a very dark green and the common green of
the hill. The soundness of this conclusion was proved,
in the summer of 1777, by the formation of a new
withered tract beyond that of the former year, which
had now passed into the decayed or black stage. Dr
Hutton attempted no explanation of the phenomena
;
but he felt convinced that they were not explained
by reference to electricity or to insects, for how should
either of these causes operate in so peculiar a manner
as to both time and local situation?
About this time, the opinion that fairy circles were
produced by lightning, was adopted by several emi-
nent men. Priestley advocated it in one of his works,
and it was advanced with confidence in the "Botanic
Garden" of Dr Darwin, who argued that a stream of
electricity, issuing from a cloud, and penetrating the
earth, would be drawn out into a cylindrical form, as
loose wool is when drawn out into a thread, and would
strike the ground from two to ten yards in diameter;
and that, "as a stream of electricity displaces the air
it passes through, it was plain no part of the grass
could be calcined by it, but just the external ring of
that cylinder where the grass could have access to the
air, since, without air, nothing can be calcined." These
assertions were all made with perfect confidence, and
no one seemed to think it necessary that any observa-
tions or experiments should be made upon the rings
themselves, with the view of settling the question. It
is really remarkable to find men, so lately as fifty
years ago, giving themselves up to endless blind specu-
lation on a point which was evidently within the reach
of observation, and could be settled by no other means.
As the further history of the question illustrates
the state of science and also of mind at that time, we
shall make no apology for going on to remark, that
the first approach to the truth seems to have been
made by a gentleman writing from Kendal, under the
signature "J. G.," and whose letter appears in the
Gentleman's Magazine for January 1791. He ob-
serves, that the causes producing fairy rings destroy
the grass, root and stem. The decay of the vegetable
matter enriches the soil, and is the main cause, he
conceives, of the luxuriance of the grass when it again
grows on the place. The new grass is produced by
seeds advancing from the restored or healthy border
within, as the edges of a green walk in a garden en-
croach on the land contiguous to them. Why is not
new grass propagated, in like manner, from the other
side upon the withered belt? Evidently because the
withered tracts is occasioned by each tract being
cessively deprived of some principle of vegetation;"
but how it is so affected, he does not attempt to ex-
plain. In the autumn of the ensuing year, a letter
from a Mr Crocker, dated at Frome School, gives
us the first account, after Hutton's, of any exact ob-
servations being made on the rings. He states, that,
a twelvemonth before, he had set down in a plan the
exact situations of a number of the circles in the pad-
dock behind his house, some of which then bore fungi,
both of the poisonous and esculent kinds. On taking
up a spadeful of the earth, it was found full of the
spawn of these fungi. He also observed places which
were mere spots of a few inches diameter, where the
grass was beginning to wither in the centre, and
where he likewise found the spawn of fungi. These
he thought the origins of fairy circles. He con-
cluded that the fungi were the cause of the tem-
porary extinction of the herbage which constitutes
a fairy ring. The fungi growing on one of the iso-
lated spots would decay in winter, so as to leave the
ground ready to give forth new herbage by the next
season. Meanwhile, "the spawn of the fungi extends
itself to the circumjacent soil, in search of the vegeta-
tive principle necessary to its continuance, and forms
the first ring round the last year's spot. This now
forms a barren circle, or a fairy ring, of one year's
growth. The spawn in this ring performing the same
operation as the last year's spot had done, a second
barren circle appears; and the spawn spreading itself
further, in search of proper nutriment, forms, in the
following year, a larger ring than the last." And so
on, he says, the process will go, a wider circle being
formed every year. This is, in reality, very nearly a
full explanation of the mystery, and its being so is
particularly instructive, when we consider that Mr
Crocker was the first speculator on the subject who
had given the matter of investigation a studious and
exact attention.
The complete theory of fairy rings was given to the
Royal Society in 1807, by the illustrious Wollaston,
who does not appear to have been aware of Mr
Crocker's views. Living for some years in the country,
he had an opportunity of observing the phenomenon
in some instances. In a set of circles of small dia-
meter, he found certain fungi growing immediately
on the outside of the circle of dark grass. This led
him to suppose that "progressive increase from a cen-
tral point was the probable mode of the formation of
the ring." He "thought it not improbable that the
soil which had once contributed to the support of
fungi, might be so exhausted of some peculiar pabulum
necessary for their production, as to be rendered in-
capable of producing a second crop of that singular
class of vegetables. The second year's crop would con-
sequently appear in a small ring surrounding the ori-
ginal centre of vegetation; and at every succeeding
year, the defect of nutriment on one side would neces-
sarily cause the new roots to extend themselves solely
in the opposite direction, and would occasion the circle
of fungi continually to proc
from the centre outwards. An appearance of luxu-
riance of the grass would follow as a natural conse-
proceed by by annual enlargement
quence, as the soil of an interior circle would always
be enriched by the decayed roots of the fungi 
preceding year's growth." These views were supported
by the results of observation, and have never been
controverted.
"During the growth of the fungi," he says, "they
so 
entirely absorb all nutriment from the soil beneath,
that the herbage is for a while destroyed, and a ring
appears bare of grass surrounding the dark ring. If
a transverse section be made of the soil beneath the
ring at this time, the part beneath the fungi appears
paler than the soil on either side of it; but that which
is beneath the interior circle of dark grass is found,
on the contrary, to be considerably darker than the
general surrounding soil. But in the course of a few
weeks after the fungi have ceased to appear, the soil
where they stood grows darker, and the grass soon
vegetates again with peculiar vigour." "For the pur-
pose," he adds, "of observing the progress of various
circles, I marked them three or four years in succes-
sion, by incisions of different forms, by which I could
distinguish clearly the successive annual increase, and
I found it to vary in different circles from eight inches
to as much as two feet. The broadest rings that I
have seen were those of the common mushroom (Ag.
campestris); the narrowest are the most frequent,
and are those of the champignon (Ag. orcades of
Dr Withering). The mushroom, accordingly, makes
circles of largest diameter; but those of the cham-
pignon are the most regular. There are, however, as
many as three other fungi that exhibit the same mode
of extension, and produce the same effect upon the
herbage. These are the Ag. terreus, Ag. procerus, and
the Lycoperdon bovista, the last of which is far more
common than the two last-mentioned agarics.
There is one circumstance," continues Dr Wollas-
ton, "which may be frequently observed respecting
these circles, which can be satisfactorily accounted
for, according to the preceding hypothesis of the cause
of their increase, and may be considered as a confir-
mation of its truth. Whenever two adjacent circles
are found to interfere, they not only do not cross each
other, but both circles are invariably obliterated be
tween the points of contact: at least, in more than
twenty cases, I have no one instance to the contrary.

also not unworthy of observation, that different species
of fungi appear to require the same nutriment; for
in a case of interference between one circle of puff-
balls and another of mushrooms, they did not inter-
sect. I found once that a tree had interrupted the
regular progress of a circle; but this appeared to be
only a temporary impediment, as the extension had
proceeded at the usual rate, and by passing obliquely
from each side into the soil beyond the tree, had given
the ring the form of a kidney, so that another year
or two would probably re-unite the two extremities
into one curve surrounding the tree."
We trust that the fairy rings, which have so long
been regarded with superstitious feelings by the un-
educated, and are perhaps to this day a mystery to
many of the enlightened, are now satisfactorily ex-
plained. The explanation takes away a romantic
dream of the popular mind; but it substitutes a
better and more legitimate wonder, in tracing one of
those beautiful arrangements of providence by which
the fruits of the earth are made to grow each after
its kind. We here see a lively example of that ex-
haustion of the food appropriate to particular species
of plants, and that necessary and natural rotation of
crops, which man is called on to take an enlightened
advantage of, if he would cultivate the soil with suc-
cess. The length at which we have given the history
of the investigation will not be too much, if we have
thereby, in the least degree, illustrated the absurdity
of speculation without observation, and how it is only
by the latter that any progress can be made in natural
science.

OF all kinds of facts, there are none so difficult to be
obtained as facts about foreign countries; yet books
of travel abound in a proportion far greater than those
on any other subject. The reason of this is pithily
explained by Captain Alexander in his work on Por-
tugal: "There are," he says, "more false facts than
false theories in the world;" and no class of authors
are so liable to promulgate the former, with an im-
plicit belief in their truth, as the general run of tra-
vellers. In traversing other quarters of the globe,
Europeans see everything with European eyes, judging
of manners, institutions, and even of scenery, by their
own standards. Nay, in many instances, absurdities
are decried of which they themselves are guilty. The
German student, for example, with his hair hanging
half-way down his back, will make himself merry at the
expense of the long queue of a Chinese; and we have
seen a work on South America, in which the practice
followed by the Butucodos tribe, of fastening pieces of
cork into their chins, was much ridiculed by its Por-
tuguese author, whose portrait, opposite the title page,
exhibited himself adorned with a pair of ear-rings!
He whose statements are to be most confidently
relied on, is the traveller who has lived for some time
in the country upon which he writes; who has resided
there long enough to find out the constant, general
habits of the people; and who is a a sufficient master of
their language to dive into their prejudices, and to com-
physical and moral, those prejudices have been formed;
able to communicate what facts he has acce
in a clear and forcible manner, and so as not to
make them appear like a laboured collection of sta-
them with his to see under what influences,
having himself of such knowledge, to be
tistics. He must do more than drily assert-he must
paint; not with the gaudy colours of exaggeration,
but with the sober tints of truth.
This brings us to M. Kohl, who possesses all the
qualifications we have named; but the last in a pre-
ponderating degree. He is, in the widest signification
which his long residence in Russia enabled him to
collect, is imparted to the reader with the fullest effect.
He does not relate merely, but he dramatises. When
he has an anecdote to repeat, he makes the most of it;
words, a literary artist ; the fund of information
brings it to a climax, so that it may tell. When
he has to describe, he places his reader in such a situa-
tion, as enables him to form in his own mind a picture
of the place the author is portraying. An example of
this occurs in the first chapter. M. Kohl wants to
show us the city of St Petersburg; and he does not
after the fashion of those dull writers of travels, who
take guide-books as their model for style-tell us the
city contains so many streets, which are so wide in
some places, and so narrow in others; but he takes us
by the hand, and ascending an elevated tower, exhibits
a panoramic view of the splendid array of palaces,
monuments, and streets, of which the city consists,
with the glorious river Neva gliding through it. In
looking from this high position, he goes on to observe,
that "the length of the open spaces bordered by the
public buildings, is not much less than an English
mile; and the spectacles, metamorphoses, living pic-
tures, and phantasmagoria, which daily and hourly
present themselves to the spectator who keeps watch
upon the tower of the Admiralty, are as varied as they
are magnificent and interesting. The rattling of im-
perial equipages scarcely ceases for a moment. Field-
marshals, generals, governors, and gentlemen of the
court, are constantly coming and going. Priestly
processions, military parades, pompous equipages, and
